name: だるまときんぎょ (Daruma to Kingyo)

claims.text: This is an oden specialist, and oden is the core of the menu. Oden is simmered in a shared dashi broth, so ingredients sit and cross-contaminate in one communal pot. No gluten-free menu or allergen labeling is documented, and a celiac should not assume any item is safe here.
Wheat-containing oden items are central to the offering, including the nankan-age (fried tofu) and other fried pieces, all of which share the same dashi pot.

Oden dashi is typically built on soy sauce, and most Japanese soy sauce contains wheat. The broth here is described as the foundation of nearly every dish, including the signature potato salad and dishes where the dashi is worked into unexpected preparations, so wheat-based seasoning is likely present throughout. Not celiac-safe.

The dashi is a traditional oden broth, which generally relies on bonito (katsuobushi) alongside kombu, making it not vegan even for vegetable items. Vegetable oden such as daikon, tomato, and avocado is simmered in this same animal-based broth, so vegans should confirm directly and treat these as not vegan by default.

There is a genuine focus on fresh, seasonal vegetable oden (daikon, tomato, avocado and more), so plant-forward diners without a strict animal-product or gluten restriction have appealing options to discuss with staff.

name: 呑龍 淀店 (Donryu Yodo-ten (Tonryu Yodo))

claims.text: This is a town-Chinese (machi-chuka) kitchen built around gyoza, ramen, fried rice, stir-fries, and fried dishes like karaage and sweet-and-sour pork. These rely heavily on wheat (gyoza wrappers, ramen noodles, batter/flour dusting) and soy-based sauces, and everything is cooked on shared woks, surfaces, and frying oil. Assume cross-contamination throughout; it is not celiac-safe.

Sauces and seasonings across the menu (fried rice, stir-fries, gyoza dipping, ramen broth, tenshinhan) are soy-sauce based, and standard Japanese soy sauce is brewed with wheat. No gluten-free soy sauce is documented.

No vegan or vegetarian options are documented. Broths and dishes at a machi-chuka spot are typically pork/chicken-based, and the kitchen shares woks and oil across meat dishes, so cross-contact with animal products should be assumed. Vegan diners should confirm directly with staff.
Reviewers describe warm, comfortable service and note that staff can be flexible with some menu modifications, so it is worth speaking with them directly about your needs.
Not gluten-free or celiac-safe. The gyoza here are wheat-flour wrappers, and the shop's whole identity is thin-skinned dumplings, so wheat is central to nearly every dish.

This is a tiny roughly ten-seat counter kitchen wrapping and char-cooking wheat dumplings to order on shared surfaces, so flour and cross-contact should be assumed throughout. No gluten-free accommodation is documented.

The signature dipping sauce is a rich miso-based sauce, and miso plus typical Japanese seasonings commonly contain wheat and soy. Treat the sauces and seasonings as containing wheat and soy unless staff confirm otherwise.
Not suitable for vegans. The dumplings are built around Kagoshima black pork, and originals add egg yolk (negi gyoza). Fillings, sauces, and the shared kitchen all involve animal products.

This is not a celiac-safe restaurant. The entire menu centers on beef tendon and oxtail simmered in a hatcho-miso (fermented soybean) broth served as miso-nikomi oden -- a wheat/soy/dashi-heavy style. Oden items commonly contain wheat, and everything cooks in one large shared simmering pot, so cross-contamination is inherent and unavoidable.

All dishes share a single communal nikomi pot visible at the front of the shop, so any gluten-free item would be cooked in the same broth as wheat-containing oden and miso. No separate or dedicated preparation is indicated.

The signature broth is built on hatcho miso (fermented soybean), and izakaya beef/oden cooking of this style typically also involves soy sauce, most of which contains wheat. Soy is core to the dish and cannot be avoided here.

Not suitable for vegans. The restaurant is a beef specialist -- the entire pot is beef tendon and oxtail simmered for hours -- and the broth is built around and saturated with beef. There are no documented plant-based options, and the deliberately tiny menu offers no meat-free alternative.

name: 本格手打うどん 大河 (Honkaku Teuchi Udon Taiga)

claims.text: This is a handmade wheat-flour udon shop where flour is kneaded, rested and cut to order throughout service, so airborne and surface flour contact is unavoidable. It is not celiac-safe.
Tempura is a core part of the menu and the batter is wheat flour mixed with dashi, fried in shared oil alongside the udon operation, so fried items are not gluten-free.
Broths and bukkake/tsuyu sauces are dashi- and soy-sauce based. Most Japanese soy sauce and tsuyu contain wheat, so the seasonings should be assumed to contain gluten unless staff confirm otherwise.

The dashi-based broths contain seafood derivatives (bonito/kelp dashi), and the tempura batter is made with secondary dashi, so even vegetable tempura is not vegan. No vegetarian or vegan menu is documented.
Seasonal vegetable tempura, including local Fukakusa bamboo shoots in spring, is a highlight for diners without wheat restrictions.

This is not a celiac-safe restaurant. The signature saba-ni is simmered for days in a tare of soy sauce, sake, mirin, and sugar, and the teishoku meals are dashi- and soy-heavy. No gluten-free menu or accommodation is indicated anywhere in available sources.

The recommended set includes fried items (chicken cutlet and croquette) served alongside the saba-ni, so even non-saba dishes carry gluten and likely shared-oil risk. No dedicated gluten-free fryer is documented.
The mackerel's simmering tare is explicitly made with soy sauce (shoyu); most Japanese soy sauce is brewed with wheat, so the dish should be treated as containing gluten.

Not suitable for vegans or vegetarians. The kitchen is built around fish (simmered mackerel), and the teishoku also include meat (chicken cutlet) and egg (tamagoyaki). The base broths rely on fish-based dashi. No plant-based options are indicated.

name: いのうえの餃子 (Inoue no Gyoza)

claims.text: This is not a celiac-safe restaurant. The core menu is gyoza with wheat-flour wrappers, plus wheat-noodle ramen and other town-Chinese dishes, so gluten is unavoidable and there are no documented gluten-free options.

Fried items such as fried chicken (often wheat-battered or flour-dusted) are served alongside gyoza and curry from a small shared kitchen, so heavy cross-contamination of wheat should be assumed; no separate gluten-free preparation is documented.

The ramen is described as soy-sauce (shoyu) based, and Chinese-style cooking here relies on soy sauce, which in Japan almost always contains wheat. Assume soy sauce throughout the menu is not gluten-free.

Not suitable for vegans or vegetarians. The menu is built around pork gyoza, fried chicken, char siu ramen and meat-based dishes, with pork and likely meat or fish-based broths and dashi seasonings pervasive. No plant-based options are documented.

No allergen handling, ingredient sourcing, or dietary-accommodation information is documented for this shop. Diners with celiac disease or strict dietary needs should confirm directly with the owner before visiting.

Not celiac-safe. Okonomiyaki here is a wheat-flour batter and yakisoba uses wheat noodles, both cooked on a shared teppan (flat grill) - the core menu is wheat-based with no gluten-free option indicated.
The okonomiyaki batter is described as being made with dashi and grated mountain yam in addition to wheat flour, so even the batter carries dashi (commonly fish-based) on top of the gluten.

Okonomiyaki and yakisoba are finished with okonomiyaki/soba sauce, which is typically soy-sauce based; most Japanese soy sauce and okonomiyaki sauce contain wheat, adding another gluten source beyond the batter and noodles.
Not vegan-friendly. The okonomiyaki batter contains dashi and egg, and the dishes are built with pork belly, seasoned ground beef and squid; the shared teppan also cooks meat and seafood.
